title: Accounts Merge
pattern: Union-Find / BFS over an email graph
statement:
You are given a list of account records. Each record is an array of strings: the first string is the account holder's name and every remaining string is an email address listed on that record. Two records belong to the same person whenever they share at least one email address, and they also belong together through a chain of records that share emails with each other.

Merge every set of records that belongs to the same person into a single group. A group is an array whose first element is the group's name and whose remaining elements are all the distinct emails of the group, sorted in ascending lexicographic order.

The name of a group is the name of the earliest record in the input, meaning the record with the smallest index, that belongs to that group. A record that lists no email addresses at all forms a group containing only its name.

Return the groups sorted by name, and for two groups that share a name, ordered by their email lists compared from the first email onwards. An email never appears twice inside a group.

Constraints: `1 <= accounts.length <= 8`, `1 <= accounts[i].length <= 8` and `1 <= accounts[i][j].length <= 12`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Which record an email came from does not matter in the end. What matters is which emails are tied together into one connected chunk.
Two records end up together when a chain of shared emails connects them, which is exactly connectivity in a graph whose vertices are emails and whose edges join the emails sitting on one record.

Give every email a representative (union-find, or one BFS per unvisited email to collect its whole component), merge the emails of each record under one representative, then bucket the emails by representative and sort every bucket.

editorial.approach: The brute force keeps a list of groups and walks the records in input order. For a new record it scans every existing group and collects the ones that share at least one email with the record, merges all of the collected groups plus the record into one group, and keeps the name of the earliest record among them. Collecting every overlapping group in the same pass is what makes a single pass sufficient: the email set of the merged group is exactly the union of the sets that were collected, and any group overlapping that union overlaps one of the collected groups, so it would already have been collected. The optimal version performs the same merging with a disjoint-set forest. Every email string becomes a node, all emails of one record are unioned together, and afterwards the emails are bucketed under their representative. The group name is attached by walking the records a second time in input order and writing the record's name onto its representative the first time that representative shows up, which is exactly the earliest record rule. Buckets are then sorted by name and by email list.
editorial.why_optimal: Let n be the total number of email strings in the input. Reading the input once is unavoidable, and the output must present every group's emails in ascending order, so the emitted answer alone forces a comparison sort that costs O(n log n). Union-find with path compression brings the merge work down to amortised near-constant time per email, so the whole solution sits at O(n log n) and no stronger bound is available. The brute force pays an extra factor of n across the declared limits because it rescans the growing group list for every record, which is O(n²).
editorial.pitfalls: Records that list only a name, records that repeat the same email twice, and records that merge while carrying different names, where the tie must go to the earliest record index rather than to the most recent one seen. The outer order compares names first and email lists second, so the emails must be sorted before that comparison or two correct implementations disagree on the emitted order. A union-find that records the name at the moment an email is inserted, before all unions have finished, can attach the name to a representative that later stops being the root. The path compression loop must stop when the parent already points at the root, otherwise it walks one step too far.
